en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Bhūtagāmavagga 18.
The Training Rule on the Upper Story Hut.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, two monks were staying in an upper chamber of a dwelling belonging to the Sangha; one was below and one was above.
The monk on the upper level sat down suddenly upon a bed with detachable legs.
A leg of the bed broke off and struck the head of the monk who was below.
Then that bhikkhu cried out.
The bhikkhus ran up to him and said this to him:
“Why did you cry out, friend?”
Then that bhikkhu reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before]... were indignant, disparaged it, and complained:
"How can a bhikkhu suddenly sit down on a bed with detachable legs in an upper story of a cell belonging to the Saṅgha?"
Then those monks, having rebuked that monk in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… Is it true, monk, that you suddenly sat down on a bed with detachable legs in an upper chamber of a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, suddenly sit down on a bed with detachable legs in an upper chamber of a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so forth].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

“Whosoever, however, a monk should sit down or lie down on a bed or a bench with detachable legs in an upper story chamber of a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, however:
Whoever such as this...
[as above] ...is called a "bhikkhu"... [as above] ...this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu."
A "monastery belonging to the Sangha" (saṅghika) is one that has been given to and dedicated to the Sangha.
A "pavilion in the air" (vehāsakuṭi) is called...
It is at the height of a medium-sized man’s head.
A bed with a foot-strike is one that stands fixed by piercing it through its frame.
A "stool with fixed legs" is one that stands by being fixed into its parts.
"Should sit down" means...
If she sits down on it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"She lies down on it" means:
if she lies down on it, there is an offense of expiation.

If, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, one perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, and sits down or lies down on a bed or a bench with legs that touch the ground in an upper chamber, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha,

one is doubtful … [as above] … if, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, one perceives it as belonging to an individual, and sits down or lies down on a bed or a bench with legs that touch the ground in an upper chamber, there is an offense of expiation.
If it belongs to an individual, but one perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it belongs to an individual, but one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it belongs to an individual, but one perceives it as belonging to an individual, yet it belongs to another individual, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense regarding one's own private property.
There is no offense in the case of a hut for storing firewood.
Below the leaden clapper, it is unusable;
it is a heap of paving stones.
If a curtain has been given,
and one standing there takes hold of it or fastens it on,
except in the case of one who is insane.
"For the first offender":
thus ends the eighth training rule concerning the upper-story hut.
